name: Front camera distortion

lead: Front camera distortion refers to how photos taken very close to the face, as selfies usually are, change the apparent proportions of facial features. Features nearest the lens, notably the nose, look larger relative to ears and the rest of the head.

People who care about how they look in photos use this idea to get more representative pictures: shooting from a greater distance, using a longer lens or the rear camera, or zooming in. The underlying optics are standard photography principles about camera distance.

paras: Common habits include holding the phone farther away and cropping or zooming, using the rear camera with a timer or a helper, using a tripod, or using a portrait-range lens setting. Users also compare their selfie face with how they look in photos taken from a distance or in a mirror.

There is no physical risk. The practical caveat commonly noted is that people judge their faces differently depending on source image, so close-range photos can look different from how others see them in person.

angle.text: Changing the camera distance changes how facial proportions appear in the image. People use farther shots or longer lenses to present their face more as it appears in person.

lead: Front camera distortion is the idea that selfie photos, taken at short distance with a wide-angle phone lens, alter facial proportions. In photography the effect is attributed to camera-to-subject distance rather than the lens alone: two shots from the same position show the same perspective, regardless of lens [1].

Wikipedia's article on perspective distortion notes that wide-angle portraits taken up close can make the nose look too large and distort expression, while longer lenses from farther away give a flatter look; 85 to 135 mm lenses on a 35 mm camera are generally regarded as good portrait lenses [1].
In looksmaxxing and photo-presentation circles the concept is used to explain why a person may look different in selfies than in photos taken by others, and why some prefer rear-camera shots.
infobox: Shoot from farther away or with a longer lens [1]

paras: Perspective in an image depends mainly on distance. Close shots with wide lenses exaggerate depth, so nearby objects appear disproportionately large; distant shots with telephoto lenses compress depth [1]. A selfie is taken at roughly arm's length, so features closer to the lens, such as the nose, are rendered larger relative to features farther back, such as the ears. Wikipedia's article does not discuss selfies specifically; applying its principles to arm's-length phone photos is a common reading of them.

The belief drives habits such as using the rear camera, shooting at distance and cropping, and comparing mirror view, selfie and third-party photos when assessing facial features. It also features in discussions of why people dislike how they look in selfies.
No studies found in the sources compiled for this entry. Photography references describe the underlying perspective principle [1].
